case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a user of a free sports news website qualifies as a 'consumer' under the Video Privacy Protection Act (VPPA), and whether the disclosure of their video-viewing data to third parties constitutes a cognizable statutory violation.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Video Privacy Protection Act (VPPA), 18 U.S.C. § 2710, specifically the definitions of 'consumer' under § 2710(a)(1) and 'personally identifiable information' under § 2710(a)(3), as well as the wrongful disclosure provision under § 2710(b)(1)
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Michael Salazar argues that the Sixth Circuit incorrectly interpreted the VPPA's definition of 'consumer,' creating a circuit split that only the Supreme Court can resolve. He contends this case is the superior vehicle for resolving the split — compared to the pending NBA petition (No. 24-994) — because it arrives with a final judgment, on a clean record, with no ongoing proceedings below. He further argues that the Sixth Circuit's statutory interpretation is misguided and inconsistent with the text of the VPPA, and that every VPPA violation presents a concrete, cognizable injury sufficient for Article III standing.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Paramount Global (247Sports) argues that certiorari should be denied for multiple independent reasons: (1) 247Sports is a free sports news website, not a video tape rental service, and is categorically outside the VPPA's intended scope; (2) Salazar's complaint fails as a matter of law under the controlling precedent of every circuit that has addressed the dispositive issues; (3) the 'consumer' question is not outcome-determinative because the complaint fails for additional independent reasons that would complicate further review; (4) the issues should be allowed to continue percolating in the lower courts, particularly given ongoing litigation in the Second Circuit regarding the 'personally identifiable information' standard; and (5) this Court recently rejected judge-made atextual tests, which may affect how the Second Circuit revisits its 'ordinary person' standard on remand.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Jackson's argument that the Sixth Circuit improperly inserted 'audio visual' before 'goods or services' — a form of judicial interpolation condemned in A.J.T. v. Osseo Area Schools — is the strongest challenge to my position, and I acknowledge it has genuine textual force. However, even accepting that the Sixth Circuit's specific rationale was imprecisely articulated, the judgment below remains defensible on independent noscitur a sociis grounds: 'subscriber' read alongside 'renter' and 'purchaser' still connotes a transactional relationship that a free website visitor does not satisfy, regardless of whether the majority below used the precise statutory language. Justice Sotomayor's surplusage argument under Duncan v. Walker is the most intellectually serious challenge — if 'consumer' already required a video transaction, the PII definition's separate reference to 'requested or obtained specific video materials' may do redundant work — but as Justice Alito correctly observes, that provision can be read as defining what information is protected once consumer status is established, not as expanding who qualifies as a consumer. My minimalist instincts are reinforced by the vehicle concerns: with Solomon v. Flipps Media percolating in the Second Circuit and the NBA petition presenting a cleaner vehicle, granting certiorari here risks an advisory ruling that resolves only one prong of a multi-pronged dismissal without actually determining the litigation.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor raises the most serious textual challenge — that the Sixth Circuit's insertion of 'audio visual' before 'goods or services' creates surplusage problems and rewrites the statute — and Justice Jackson echoes this concern by noting our recent decisions in A.J.T. v. Osseo Area Schools rejecting judge-made atextual glosses. I take this seriously, but it does not ultimately move me: even accepting that the Sixth Circuit's 'audio visual' limitation was imprecise, the more fundamental textual question is whether Salazar qualifies as a 'subscriber' at all, and under noscitur a sociis, 'subscriber' must be read alongside 'renter' and 'purchaser' — all three terms presupposing a transactional relationship involving consideration or commitment, which a free website visitor simply does not have. The original public meaning of 'subscriber' in 1988 carried connotations of a formal, typically paid, ongoing relationship, as Justice Barrett correctly observes, and the VPPA's legislative genesis in the Bork video rental controversy confirms Congress was targeting discrete commercial transactions with video service providers, not incidental video viewing on free news platforms. Additionally, the vehicle concerns identified by Chief Justice Roberts — that independent grounds for dismissal on PII and standing remain unresolved — counsel strongly against granting certiorari at this juncture, as we risk issuing an advisory ruling that resolves only one prong of a multi-pronged statutory question without actually determining the case.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Jackson's argument that the Sixth Circuit improperly inserted 'audio visual' before 'goods or services' — echoing A.J.T. v. Osseo Area Schools — is the strongest textual challenge to my position, and I acknowledge the Sixth Circuit's specific rationale was imprecise. However, the judgment below remains defensible on independent grounds: even correcting the Sixth Circuit's imprecision, noscitur a sociis compels reading 'subscriber' alongside 'renter' and 'purchaser,' all three of which presuppose a transactional relationship involving consideration or commitment that a passive free-website visitor simply does not provide. Justice Sotomayor's surplusage argument under Duncan v. Walker is thoughtful, but as Justice Gorsuch correctly notes, the anti-surplusage canon cannot override the associated-words canon when the latter more directly governs the disputed term's meaning — and the § 2710(a)(3) PII definition's reference to 'requested or obtained specific video materials or services' does independent work in defining what information is protected once consumer status is established, not in expanding who qualifies. The vehicle concerns Justice Kagan identifies regarding Solomon v. Flipps Media and the unresolved PII question remain independently dispositive: granting certiorari here risks an advisory ruling that resolves only one prong of a multi-pronged statutory question without actually determining the litigation.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Kagan's vehicle concern is the most serious challenge to my position — she is right that if independent PII grounds remain unresolved, a ruling on 'consumer' status alone risks being advisory. But I cannot accept that this counsels indefinite delay: the 'consumer' threshold question is logically antecedent to PII analysis, recurs in every VPPA case involving free platforms, and the Sixth-Eighth Circuit split will continue producing inconsistent results for millions of users regardless of how Solomon v. Flipps Media resolves the PII question. Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch's noscitur a sociis argument remains the strongest textual case for Respondent, but as Justice Jackson and I have both noted, that canon cannot rescue a judgment whose specific rationale — inserting 'audio visual' into a statute that contains no such limitation — constitutes precisely the judicial interpolation this Court condemned in A.J.T. v. Osseo Area Schools. The surplusage concern under Duncan v. Walker retains independent force: if 'consumer' already required a direct commercial video transaction, the PII definition's separate reference to 'requested or obtained specific video materials or services' would do no independent work, and I will not read a federal privacy statute so narrowly as to exclude the very ordinary users Congress most plausibly intended to protect.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Jackson's argument that the Sixth Circuit improperly inserted 'audio visual' before 'goods or services' remains the strongest challenge to my position, and I continue to find it textually sound — the Sixth Circuit did rewrite the statute in a way that A.J.T. v. Osseo Area Schools would condemn. However, the critical point for certiorari purposes is whether the judgment below is defensible on independent grounds, and I remain persuaded that noscitur a sociis — reading 'subscriber' alongside 'renter' and 'purchaser' — provides an independent textual basis for the outcome even if the Sixth Circuit's specific rationale was imprecise. Justice Sotomayor's surplusage argument under Duncan v. Walker is the most serious challenge to this position, but I agree with Justice Alito that the anti-surplusage concern can be resolved by recognizing that § 2710(a)(3)'s reference to 'requested or obtained specific video materials or services' does independent definitional work specifying what information is protected once consumer status is established, rather than expanding who qualifies as a consumer. The pragmatic vehicle concern — that Solomon v. Flipps Media may reshape the PII landscape before we intervene, and that a ruling here risks being advisory given the independent grounds for dismissal — continues to reinforce my judgment that denial is appropriate at this juncture.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor press the strongest counterargument — that the Sixth Circuit improperly inserted 'audio visual' before 'goods or services,' constituting the kind of judicial interpolation condemned in A.J.T. v. Osseo Area Schools, and that the anti-surplusage canon under Duncan v. Walker counsels a broader reading of 'consumer.' I take these textual concerns seriously, but they do not ultimately move me for two reasons. First, even granting that the Sixth Circuit's specific rationale was imprecisely articulated, the correct textualist analysis independently supports the same judgment: noscitur a sociis requires reading 'subscriber' in light of 'renter' and 'purchaser,' and all three terms in their 1988 ordinary public meaning connoted a transactional relationship involving consideration or commitment — a free ad-supported website visitor enters no such relationship, regardless of whether we add 'audio visual' to the statutory text or not. Second, Justice Kagan's vehicle concern remains independently dispositive for certiorari purposes: even if Salazar prevails on the 'consumer' definitional question, the unresolved PII grounds and the pending Solomon v. Flipps Media proceedings in the Second Circuit mean a ruling here risks producing an advisory opinion that resolves only one of several independent grounds for dismissal, and institutional prudence counsels waiting for the NBA petition or a cleaner vehicle where the 'consumer' question is genuinely outcome-determinative.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Jackson's argument that the Sixth Circuit improperly inserted 'audio visual' before 'goods or services' is the strongest challenge to my position, and I acknowledge it has genuine textual force — the majority below did appear to add limiting language not present in the statute, which is the kind of judicial interpolation I find troubling. However, even accepting that the Sixth Circuit's specific rationale was imprecise, the judgment below remains defensible on independent noscitur a sociis grounds: 'subscriber' read alongside 'renter' and 'purchaser' still connotes a transactional relationship that a free website visitor does not satisfy, and the anti-surplusage concern Justice Sotomayor raises can be addressed by recognizing that the PII definition's reference to 'requested or obtained specific video materials' does independent work in defining what information is protected once consumer status is established. My institutionalist instincts also counsel restraint here — with Solomon v. Flipps Media percolating in the Second Circuit and the NBA petition presenting a potentially cleaner vehicle, granting certiorari now risks an advisory ruling on an incomplete record that could undermine rather than clarify the VPPA's application across circuits. I therefore maintain my position to deny certiorari.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Jackson's textual argument — that the Sixth Circuit improperly inserted 'audio visual' before 'goods or services' in a manner this Court condemned in A.J.T. v. Osseo Area Schools — remains the strongest challenge to my position, and I continue to take it seriously. However, even granting that the Sixth Circuit's specific rationale was imprecise, the correct textualist analysis still supports the judgment below: noscitur a sociis requires reading 'subscriber' in light of its statutory companions 'renter' and 'purchaser,' all three of which connote a transactional relationship involving consideration or commitment that a passive free-website visitor simply does not provide, and this canon operates independently of whether the Sixth Circuit articulated it correctly. Justice Sotomayor's surplusage argument under Duncan v. Walker is thoughtful, but as I noted in round one, the anti-surplusage canon does not override the associated-words canon when the latter more directly governs the disputed definitional term, and the PII definition's reference to 'requested or obtained specific video materials or services' does independent work in defining what information is protected once consumer status is established rather than who qualifies as a consumer. The vehicle concerns Justice Kagan identifies — that independent PII grounds remain unresolved and Solomon v. Flipps Media is actively percolating in the Second Circuit — independently counsel against certiorari, as a ruling here risks producing an advisory opinion on an incomplete record.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch makes the strongest opposing argument — that even if the Sixth Circuit's 'audio visual' insertion was textually flawed, noscitur a sociis independently compels reading 'subscriber' alongside 'renter' and 'purchaser' as requiring transactional consideration, such that the judgment below is defensible on independent grounds. But I cannot accept this because the canon of noscitur a sociis is a tool for resolving ambiguity, not for importing requirements the text does not contain — and 'subscriber' in ordinary usage encompasses free newsletter subscribers, free platform users, and others with no monetary exchange, meaning the canon does not unambiguously resolve the question in Respondent's favor. Justice Alito's attempt to dissolve the surplusage problem by arguing that § 2710(a)(3)'s reference to 'requested or obtained specific video materials or services' does independent work defining what information is protected rather than who qualifies as a consumer is creative, but it does not fully answer Justice Sotomayor's point that the definitional structure would be oddly redundant if 'consumer' already required obtaining video materials through a transactional relationship. The vehicle concerns raised by Justices Kagan, Roberts, and Kavanaugh are legitimate institutional considerations, but a mature circuit split on a threshold definitional question affecting millions of users of free video-streaming platforms is precisely the kind of recurring issue that warrants this Court's intervention rather than indefinite deferral pending Solomon v. Flipps Media.

John Roberts.reasoning: Applying the noscitur a sociis canon as employed in Fischer v. United States and Yates v. United States, the VPPA's definition of 'consumer' as 'any renter, purchaser, or subscriber of goods or services from a video tape service provider' must be read in light of its surrounding terms — 'renter' and 'purchaser' both connote transactional, commercial relationships, which counsels against reading 'subscriber' so broadly as to encompass a user of a free website with no financial or contractual commitment. My minimalist instincts also favor denying certiorari here: the circuit split is real but still developing, the Second Circuit's reconsideration of the PII standard in Solomon v. Flipps Media may reshape the landscape, and the NBA petition presents a cleaner vehicle if the Court ultimately decides to intervene. Furthermore, Respondent's independent grounds — that the complaint fails on PII and standing bases regardless of the 'consumer' question — mean that granting cert on this narrow definitional issue risks an advisory ruling that does not resolve the broader litigation, undermining the institutional efficiency concerns that animate my preference for narrow, outcome-determinative decisions.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Applying the noscitur a sociis canon as I articulated in Fischer v. United States, the term 'consumer' in 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(1) must be read in light of the surrounding definitional structure — specifically the definition of 'video tape service provider' under § 2710(a)(4), which is anchored to the 'business' of 'rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials.' A free sports news website like 247Sports is categorically outside this transactional framework; Salazar paid nothing and entered no rental, purchase, or subscription relationship with Paramount for video goods or services, meaning he cannot qualify as a 'consumer' under the statute's plain text. The VPPA was enacted in 1988 in direct response to the Bork video rental disclosure controversy, and the original public meaning of the statute's definitional structure presupposes a commercial transactional relationship with a video tape service provider — not incidental video viewing on a free news platform. Furthermore, even setting aside the 'consumer' question, the independent grounds for dismissal identified by Respondent — including the 'personally identifiable information' standard currently percolating in the Second Circuit following this Court's rejection of judge-made atextual tests in A.J.T. v. Osseo Area Schools and Ames v. Ohio Department of Youth Services — counsel against granting certiorari at this juncture, as the issues would benefit from further development below.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: As a textualist, I find that the VPPA's definition of 'consumer' under § 2710(a)(1) — 'any renter, purchaser, or subscriber of goods or services from a video tape service provider' — must be read in its full statutory context, and the noscitur a sociis canon applied in Fischer v. United States compels the conclusion that 'goods or services' is colored by the surrounding statutory framework targeting video tape service providers in the business of renting, selling, or delivering prerecorded video content. A user of a free sports news website like 247Sports has no transactional or subscription relationship with the provider, and the three operative verbs — 'rents, purchases, or subscribes' — all connote a commercial exchange that a free website visitor simply does not engage in. Furthermore, practical consequences matter here: extending the VPPA to cover any incidental video viewing on a free news website would represent exactly the kind of textual overreach that Yates v. United States warned against, transforming a narrowly targeted privacy statute into a sweeping cause of action far beyond Congress's 1988 intent. The petition should be denied because the Sixth Circuit's judgment is defensible on textualist grounds, the record presents complicating alternative grounds for affirmance, and the better course is to allow further percolation — particularly as the Second Circuit revisits the 'personally identifiable information' standard post-A.J.T. v. Osseo Area Schools.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The VPPA's definition of 'consumer' under § 2710(a)(1) covers 'any renter, purchaser, or subscriber of goods or services from a video tape service provider,' and the Sixth Circuit's narrow reading — requiring a direct commercial transaction specifically in audiovisual goods — creates surplusage problems that the dissent below correctly identified: if 'consumer' status already requires renting or purchasing video materials, then the separate 'personally identifiable information' definition's reference to 'requested or obtained specific video materials or services' under § 2710(a)(3) does independent work only if 'consumer' is read more broadly. The rule against surplusage, as articulated in Duncan v. Walker, 533 U.S. 167 (2001), counsels against the Sixth Circuit's cramped interpretation. Moreover, the real-world impact on ordinary people who consume video content on free, ad-supported platforms — and whose viewing data is systematically disclosed to third-party trackers like Meta's Pixel — is precisely the kind of privacy harm Congress sought to prevent when enacting the VPPA, and denying these users statutory protection because they did not pay money would leave the most economically vulnerable consumers without recourse. The circuit split, now sharpened by the Eighth Circuit's analysis in Christopherson, is mature enough for this Court's resolution, and the final judgment posture of this case makes it a cleaner vehicle than the pending NBA petition.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: While I find the Sixth Circuit majority's insertion of an 'audio visual' limitation into the statutory text of § 2710(a)(1) textually suspect — as the dissent correctly notes, the statute says 'goods or services from a video tape service provider,' not 'audio visual goods or services' — I would nonetheless deny certiorari here on pragmatic vehicle grounds. The 'consumer' question, even if resolved in Salazar's favor, does not resolve the case given independent grounds for dismissal, including the 'personally identifiable information' standard currently percolating in the Second Circuit through Solomon v. Flipps Media. Under my pragmatic textualist approach, the Court benefits from allowing the PII question to develop further before taking up the VPPA's full digital-age application, and the pending NBA petition (No. 24-994) may present a cleaner vehicle. Additionally, our recent decisions in A.J.T. v. Osseo Area Schools and Ames v. Ohio Department of Youth Services rejecting judge-made atextual tests may organically reshape how lower courts approach the 'ordinary person' PII standard, warranting further percolation before this Court intervenes.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The plain text of 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(1) defines 'consumer' as a person who 'rents, purchases, or subscribes to' goods or services from a video tape service provider — three verbs that each describe a transactional relationship involving consideration or commitment. Under the associated-words canon applied in Fischer v. United States and Yates v. United States, the term 'subscribes to' cannot be stretched to encompass a user who merely visits a free, ad-supported website with no rental, purchase, or subscription transaction, because doing so would render the accompanying words 'rents' and 'purchases' contextually meaningless as limiting terms and would give 'subscribes' a meaning 'so broad that it is inconsistent with its accompanying words.' Furthermore, the VPPA's overall statutory context — anchored in the video tape rental paradigm and the 'audio visual materials' framework — confirms through noscitur a sociis that Congress was targeting discrete transactional relationships with video service providers, not passive browsing of free news websites. Denying certiorari is also appropriate on vehicle grounds, as the Second Circuit's ongoing reconsideration of the 'personally identifiable information' standard in Solomon v. Flipps Media presents an independent basis on which this case could fail, making it a poor vehicle for clean resolution of the circuit split.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Applying the noscitur a sociis canon as employed in Fischer v. United States and Yates v. United States, the VPPA's definition of 'consumer' as a 'renter, purchaser, or subscriber' must be read in light of its surrounding statutory context — a statute plainly designed to address the video tape rental industry, not free digital news platforms. The three enumerated terms ('rents, purchases, or subscribes') all connote a transactional or ongoing commercial relationship, and extending 'subscriber' to encompass any user of a free website would give that single word a breadth inconsistent with its accompanying terms and the statute's evident purpose. Moreover, as an institutionalist matter, I am persuaded by Paramount's argument that the lower courts should be permitted to continue developing this area of law, particularly given the pending Second Circuit proceedings in Solomon v. Flipps Media on the 'personally identifiable information' standard — premature intervention risks issuing guidance on an incomplete record. Consistent with the Court's recent emphasis in A.J.T. v. Osseo Area Schools and Ames v. Ohio Department of Youth Services on rejecting judge-made atextual expansions, I would deny certiorari and allow the circuit split to sharpen further before this Court intervenes.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: As a textualist, I find the statutory definition of 'consumer' under 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(1) — 'any renter, purchaser, or subscriber of goods or services from a video tape service provider' — requires careful application of noscitur a sociis, as the Court applied in Fischer v. United States (2024): 'subscriber' must be read in light of its companions 'renter' and 'purchaser,' all of which connote a transactional or financial relationship with a video tape service provider. While I am sympathetic to the dissent's concern that the Sixth Circuit majority may have improperly inserted the limiting word 'audio visual' before 'goods or services,' the more fundamental textual problem is whether a user of a free website — with no payment, no account subscription, and no ongoing transactional relationship — can plausibly be a 'subscriber' within this enumerated list; the ordinary public meaning of 'subscriber' in 1988, when the VPPA was enacted, carried connotations of a formal, typically paid, ongoing relationship. Moreover, Paramount's independent arguments — that the complaint fails on 'personally identifiable information' grounds and that the circuit split on PII is still percolating in Solomon v. Flipps Media — counsel against granting certiorari at this juncture, as the issues are not fully developed and granting review risks resolving only one prong of a multi-pronged statutory question, consistent with the Court's prudential practice reflected in Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: As a textualist-pragmatist, I am persuaded by the dissent's observation that the Sixth Circuit majority effectively rewrote 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(1) by inserting an 'audio visual' limitation before 'goods or services' that simply does not appear in the statutory text — precisely the kind of judge-made atextual gloss this Court recently rejected in A.J.T. v. Osseo Area Schools and Ames v. Ohio Department of Youth Services. The plain text of the VPPA defines 'consumer' as 'any renter, purchaser, or subscriber of goods or services from a video tape service provider,' and a registered user of a website who provides personal information in exchange for ongoing access to content fits comfortably within the ordinary meaning of 'subscriber' as recognized by dictionary definitions and the statute's broad protective purpose. My background as a public defender reinforces my concern that narrowing statutory protections through judicial interpolation disproportionately harms ordinary people who lack the resources to vindicate their privacy rights through other means, and the circuit split — with the Eighth Circuit's recent decision in Christopherson further entrenching the divide — presents exactly the kind of unresolved legal question warranting this Court's intervention. While Respondent raises legitimate concerns about vehicle quality and the pending PII question in Solomon v. Flipps Media, the final judgment posture and clean record here make this case a suitable vehicle under Virginia Military Institute v. United States.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh's vehicle concern remains the most serious challenge to my position — the independent standing and PII grounds could moot the consumer question even if we grant certiorari, producing a wasted exercise. However, I am persuaded by Justice Barrett's response that these independent grounds go to the merits of the case rather than to whether the legal question is ripe for our review; a final judgment on a stable record is precisely the kind of procedural cleanliness that makes this vehicle superior to the interlocutory NBA v. Salazar petition. Justice Thomas's noscitur a sociis argument is historically compelling — the 1988 enactment context and the Bork episode do suggest Congress had discrete commercial transactions in mind — but as Justice Gorsuch correctly notes, the canon resolves genuine ambiguity rather than licensing courts to insert limiting language Congress chose not to write, and the Sixth Circuit's effective insertion of 'audiovisual' before 'goods or services' is the kind of judicial interpolation our recent canon-against-interpolation precedents in A.J.T. and Fischer counsel against. As Chief Justice, I would assign a narrow opinion focused solely on the 'consumer' definition question, explicitly reserving the PII and standing issues, which might attract Justice Jackson and Justice Kavanaugh by addressing their vehicle concerns while avoiding the broader merits questions that divide the Court.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch make the strongest opposing argument — that the Sixth Circuit impermissibly inserted 'audiovisual' before 'goods or services,' and that courts cannot rewrite statutory text. I take this textualist concern seriously, but I believe they misapply the canon: noscitur a sociis does not insert words into the statute, it illuminates the meaning of 'subscriber' by reference to its statutory companions 'renter' and 'purchaser,' all of which connote a transactional relationship involving consideration or commitment. A person who visits a free sports news website, pays nothing, and signs no agreement is not a 'subscriber' in any sense recognizable to the public in 1988 — the word 'subscriber' in that era connoted a magazine subscription, a cable subscription, a paid ongoing commitment, not gratuitous access to a free webpage. Furthermore, the statute's title ('Wrongful disclosure of video tape rental or sale records') and the definition of 'personally identifiable information' as information identifying a person as having 'requested or obtained specific video materials' confirm that Congress was targeting discrete commercial transactions in the video rental market, not incidental viewing on free internet platforms, and I remain persuaded that certiorari should be denied to allow further percolation given the pending NBA v. Salazar and Solomon v. Flipps Media petitions.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch make the strongest opposing argument — that the Sixth Circuit inserted the word 'audiovisual' before 'goods or services,' which the statute does not contain, and that textualism forbids such judicial interpolation.
